issues.issue: Records are destroyed after seven years "except in extraordinary cases as defined by the Dean of Student Life", a standard the Dean defines after the fact and which appears nowhere else in the code. The retention period is therefore indefinite at the Dean's option.

"Within 30 class days, or as soon as practicable" makes the deadline elastic, since the alternative swallows the rule and has no measure. The definition of "class days" here (excluding summer and study abroad) also differs from 19.2, where final exams and Senior Week count as class days.

The Hearing Administrator is to ensure execution of the hearing "as prescribed in Section 23", but this code contains no Section 23; the hearing procedures are in 19.10. The governing procedural reference is therefore missing.

The bar on parties "confronting or questioning the witnesses and Accusers regarding the case prior to the hearing" cannot be squared with 19.6.e, which makes it "the responsibility of the Accuser and the Accused to notify their witnesses ... regarding the time, date, and location of the hearing". A party must contact witnesses it is forbidden to approach.

This provision lets "the Accused and Accuser" agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition, while 20.2 requires that the voting requirements be waived "by mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused". Whether the Board's consent is also needed cannot be answered from either provision alone.

"Passive assistance" is never defined, and the same provision allows the Hearing Administrator to permit "active participation by an Advisor" in "exceptional circumstances" that are not described. What an Advisor may actually do at a hearing is thus indeterminate.

The requirement that both parties be present is qualified "except as provided in Section 19.16.k", a section that does not exist in this code (the rescheduling rule is 19.6.k). The exception to the attendance requirement therefore points nowhere.

"Unduly repetitious or irrelevant" evidence may be excluded by the Board on no stated standard, and the provision expressly disclaims the rules of evidence that would supply one. What governs admissibility is left entirely to the Board.

The right "to question all witnesses appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" guaranteed here has no counterpart in the Special Examiner's Process of 22.6, which routes all Section 3 and 7 cases to an investigator who interviews witnesses separately and privately. Whether a student charged under Sections 3 or 7 retains any questioning right is unresolved by the two provisions read together.

The phrase "and only at the hearing" is grammatically attached to the right to question witnesses, so it can be read either as limiting when questioning may occur or as limiting which witnesses may be questioned. The following sentences, which admit written testimony from absentee witnesses, make the choice consequential.

Placing the burden of proof on the Accuser cannot be squared with 22.6, where the Special Examiner investigates and reports and the Dean applies a preponderance standard with no burden assigned to any party. For Section 3 and 7 cases the two allocations of proof cannot both operate.

A finding of responsibility here may be made "based only upon clear and convincing evidence", while the Standard of Evaluation in 22.6 directs that the Special Examiner's Process use preponderance of the evidence. Identical conduct is thus judged by two different standards depending on which section is charged, with no rule for mixed charges.

A blameworthy failure to attend means the Accused "shall be deemed to have accepted the responsibility", converting an absence into an admission with no finding on the merits. The provision gives the same right to a rescheduled hearing to the Accuser but imposes the deeming consequence only on the Accused.

This provision requires that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved or modified by the Dean ... or the Director", whereas the Special Examiner's Process provides that all sanctions "will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal". A student appealing under one regime is stayed and under the other is not, and nothing reconciles them.

The 2-business-day window runs from "delivery of the conduct action announcement" without saying what constitutes delivery, whereas 19.1 and 19.7 specify delivery in person, to the Brandeis e-mail account, or to the home address. When the clock starts is therefore uncertain.

Requiring students who learn of possible new evidence at the hearing to seek a continuance "rather than wait to raise the matter ... as the basis for an appeal request" operates as a waiver of the new-evidence ground expressly given by 19.7.d. Whether failing to ask for a continuance forfeits that appeal ground is not stated.

The philosophy and procedures the Chairperson explains are contained in a separate statement "available from the Department of Student Rights and Community Standards" that is not reproduced in the code. What is read to the parties is therefore governed by an external document of unknown content.

The enumerated "Rights to Fairness" — an Advisor, presenting witnesses, questioning witnesses appearing against them, verbal argument, silence — are stated as the parties' rights "under this process", yet none of them is provided in the Special Examiner's Process of 22.6, to which all Section 3 and 7 cases are sent. Whether these are University-wide fairness guarantees or only Board-hearing steps is precisely what the two provisions leave open.

The accusations read to the hearing come from the Choice of Action Form, whereas 19.1 provides that the student receives "written charges" after the Preliminary Meeting. Which document fixes the charges to be tried is not stated.

The Accused accepts or denies responsibility again at the hearing although 19.1 provides that a choice has already been made and that failure to choose "constitutes an acceptance of responsibility". What happens if the two answers differ is not addressed.

The Accused's right to question the Accuser directly at the hearing has no analogue in the Special Examiner's Process, under which Section 3 and 7 cases proceed with separate private interviews. Whether the right survives the routing rule in 3.0 and 22.6 is unresolved.

"Witnesses for the Accuser may be called" does not say who decides whether they are called, while 19.6.e conditions testimony on availability and 19.6.b leaves unlisted witnesses to the Chairperson's discretion. Whether a party may compel the calling of its own listed witness is left open.

Recall and re-questioning follow "the same order as previous witness questioning", but the orders in steps G and H are opposites, so which order governs a recalled witness is indeterminate. The provision also does not say who decides that a recall is permitted.

A finding of not responsible is announced to the parties yet the outcome notification is "pending approval by the Dean of Student Life or an Associate Dean", implying an acquittal may be withheld — while 21.1 makes Deans' approval a condition only of sanctions. Whether a not-responsible finding is final when announced cannot be settled from either provision alone.

Final sanction determinations are communicated in writing "to the Accused" only, although the Section 3 services bullet promises that the Accuser will be informed of the outcome of proceedings insofar as it relates to the Accuser. The two provisions state different disclosure obligations for the same event.

The Board is advised of the Accused's past conduct history during deliberations, although 19.6.i requires that "decisions shall be based solely upon evidence and testimony introduced at the hearing". Whether that limitation applies to the sanctioning deliberation as well as the responsibility finding is unresolved.

"The appropriate administrator" who reviews the Board's recommendations is not identified, while 21.1 names three officials who may approve or modify sanctions and 19.10.P names a further set. Who holds the reviewing authority must be pieced together from other provisions.

The SCB's jurisdiction excludes "cases related to Sections 3 and 7", but the code gives no rule for a case that charges both a Section 3 or 7 violation and violations of other sections such as 2.1. Whether the whole case goes to the Special Examiner or is split between two processes is left open.

The waiver here requires "mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused", while 19.6.c allows the Accused and Accuser alone to agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition. The two provisions state different requirements for the same waiver.
